newsitem.title: USA: Economists group sees 2.3 pct U.S. growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Economists group sees 2.3 pct U.S. growth in 1997.

text.p: The National Association of Business Economists said Monday it expected U.S. economic growth for 1997 to match this year's estimate, rising 2.3 percent, as the expansion continues to roll along.
The survey of 44 professional forecasters in November also saw inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, rising 2.9 percent this year and next.

NABE said the growth forecast was unchanged from its survey in September, although the forecasters became a little more optimistic on inflation. In September they had estimated the CPI would rise 3.0 percent in 1997.

"Moderate economic growth and low inflation will continue through 1997 and probably much longer," the group said, adding that "while all business cycles eventually end, almost all 44 economists who responded to the survey expect the economic expansion to continue for the forseeable future."

The panel lowered its forecast for interest rates. The three-month bill is expected to be 5.0 percent in December and the 30-year Treasury bond is expected to be 6.7 percent, roughtly 20 basis points lower than the September survey.

The economists said they expected the economy in the next five years to generally mirror the past five years. Overall annual growth should average 2.5 percent, productivity 1.2 percent and inflation just under 2.9 percent.
During the same period, the international value of the dollar should be flat or down, with fewer than 30 percent expecting the currency to appreciate five percent or more.
The survey also gave high marks to the Federal Reserve, with some 77 percent expressing the view that that monetary policy had been "about right" over the past six months.

Some 57 percent believed there should be no change in monetary policy over the next six months, while 24 percent preferred a more stimulative stance and 18 percent thought it should be more restrictive, the economist group said.

The survey also found that the majority of the panel believed the so-called non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment was in the 4.5 to 5.5 percent range, down from 10 years ago, reflecting increased domestic and international competition.

The unemployment rate, which hit 5.2 percent in October, would be about 5.4 percent for all of this year and 5.5 percent in 1997. Nonfarm payroll jobs are predicted to rise 1.5 percent next year, slower than a 2.0 percent rise this year.

The report noted that the advisory committee on the consumer price index is due to make its report to the Senate Finance Committee and was widely expected to say that the CPI overstates inflation by 1 percent.

The survey of economists found that most believe Congress should incorporate that conclusion in cost-of-living formulas which govern individual tax brackets, federal benefit payments and the Treasury's upcoming inflation-adjusted bonds.
